title: Same forest, different story: Beetle community responses to non‐native tree species depend on the vertical stratum
content:
Our findings emphasize the importance of integrating vertical stratification into biodiversity monitoring for a comprehensive understanding of the ecological impacts of climate-adapted forest management with non-native tree species. Promoting mixed stands can mitigate negative biodiversity impacts of non-native tree species and support the maintenance of multidimensional biodiversity of associated forest biota under climate-driven forest reorganization.


Abstract

Increased forest diebacks under climate change necessitate adaptation strategies of forest management, which often include the use of drought-resistant non-native tree species. However, their planting has raised concerns about the ecological impacts on forest biodiversity and functioning. Relevant studies are largely limited to single forest strata, often focusing on ground or subcanopy communities, which prevents a comprehensive understanding of how biodiversity responds to changes in native and non-native tree species identity and composition across forest strata. Here, we provide a synthesis of how the introduction of North American Douglas fir alters different facets of biodiversity across vertical strata in Central European forests. We focused on beetles, a hyperdiverse group of forest biota, and considered economically important stand types including and excluding Douglas fir, namely, monocultures and mixtures of native European beech, native Norway spruce planted outside its natural range and non-native Douglas fir. Beetle diversity varied strongly among forest strata and stand types. Douglas fir monocultures consistently supported lower taxonomic, functional and phylogenetic diversity at both local (plot) and regional (landscape) scales compared with the other stand types, with the most pronounced differences observed in the canopy. Mixture effects depended on the identity of admixed conifers: beech–spruce mixtures favoured beetle diversity on the forest floor, whereas beech–Douglas fir mixtures generally buffered canopy beetle diversity losses observed in Douglas fir monocultures. Canopy openness, deadwood volume and tree neighbourhood diversity shaped biodiversity across all strata. Subcanopy communities generally depended most on environmental features, while canopy communities were strongly driven by tree species identity. Community composition and feeding-guild structure diverged with increasing stratum height, especially when comparing beech- and conifer-dominated stands, underscoring the sensitivity of canopy assemblages to host tree identity due to their direct contact with tree-specific habitats and resources. Synthesis and applications. Our findings emphasize the importance of integrating vertical stratification into biodiversity monitoring for a comprehensive understanding of the ecological impacts of climate-adapted forest management with non-native tree species. Promoting mixed stands can mitigate negative biodiversity impacts of non-native tree species and support the maintenance of multidimensional biodiversity of associated forest biota under climate-driven forest reorganization.
